column4: God's emphatic splitting of the earth is the Quran's literal counterpart to the section's ploughed, opened field.
The question about what people till stages the very act hidden in the section's agricultural sense of falah.
The next question assigns the crop's growth to God rather than the sower, matching growth received through divine blessing.
Fruit-bearing gardens are followed by the command to give the produce's due on harvest day, exactly the section's grown crop and paid share.
The afterlife is a tilth whose yield God increases, while worldly tilth gives no afterlife share; this states the section's two fields and two outcomes.
Giving one's wealth in order to purify oneself makes the paid share and tazakka one act.
Success and purification meet in the same formula as 87:14, now with the soul as the thing cultivated.
The community is a crop that sends out its shoot, strengthens, thickens, and stands on its stalk, a full picture of blessed growth that does not become chaff.
The charity taken from wealth both cleans and causes growth, expressed by تطهرهم وتزكيهم بها; it directly explains how the share purifies what remains.
Spending wealth is pictured as one grain producing seven ears and multiplied seed, joining gift, crop, and increase.
Sincere spending is a high garden whose rain brings double yield, so giving itself becomes fruitful cultivation.
God effaces usury but makes charities grow, the sharpest non-field statement of increase through giving rather than grasping.
Interest meant to increase wealth does not increase with God, whereas zakat given for His face makes its givers the multipliers.
The orchard owners resolve that no poor person will enter at harvest, directly reversing the command to give the crop's due.
After withholding the poor person's share, the owners recognize that they themselves have been deprived of the yield.
خَرَاجُ رَبِّكَ خَيْرٌ joins the section's named kharaj form to the Lord, what is better, and the One who provides.
بَقِيَّتُ ٱللَّهِ خَيْرٌ names the God-given remainder as better after honest dealing, closely matching the clean remainder of a paid due.
Believers must spend from good earnings and from what God brings out of the earth, making the field's produce the substance of the gift.
Good soil yields by its Lord's permission while bad soil yields only meager growth, a direct distinction between two outcomes on the earth.
Adjoining plots receive the same water yet differ in fruit, sharpening the section's contrast between fields sharing one ground.
The command that a person look at his food opens the very field process the section asks the reader to see inside 87:14.
Water is poured abundantly before the earth is split and planted, supplying the first action in the explicit field scene.
After splitting the earth, God makes grain grow in it; the opened ground becomes productive rather than waste.
Grapes and herbage specify what the split earth produces in the continuing field scene begun in 80:25-27.
Olives and date palms add cultivated, fruit-bearing plants to the yield of the opened earth.
Dense gardens show the split ground completed as tended and abundant cultivation.
Fruit and pasture distinguish human produce and grazing growth within the same divinely watered scene.
The whole yield is identified as provision for people and their livestock, stating the purpose of the productive field.
God could turn the crop into shattered dry matter, explicitly placing the tilled field under the pasture's chaff-like fate.
The ruined crop leaves the growers confessing that they are deprived, naming the lost share and remainder of a failed harvest.
The tested garden owners swear to cut their fruit in the morning, beginning a harvest scene governed by their handling of its due.
A visitation from the Lord circles the garden while they sleep, reversing their assumed control over its yield.
By morning the garden has become like a field already stripped or blackened, the withheld harvest made unavailable.
Their own summons to go early and cut the crop keeps the moral failure fixed on an actual harvest.
They approach confident that they can prevent access, making exclusion from the yield part of the planned harvest.
The most balanced owner asks why they did not glorify God, bringing the field failure into the stance commanded by سَبِّحْ.
They finally glorify their Lord and confess wrongdoing, recognizing the true Master of the garden after its loss.
Their admission of transgression identifies moral failure, rather than bad technique, as the cause illuminated by the ruined yield.
They hope their Lord will replace the garden with a better one and turn back to Him, joining divine husbandry, loss, and better replacement.
The garden's earthly punishment is set beside the greater afterlife punishment, extending the harvest scene into the two destinies of 87:16-17.
Gardens of lasting residence are named as the reward of the one who purifies himself, giving tazakka a garden and an enduring outcome.
The declaration that the believers have attained falah supplies the result later specified by their performance of zakat.
Within the portrait of those who attain falah, this ayah singles out those who actively perform zakat.
Giving the relative, needy person, and traveler their right leads directly to the declaration that those givers are the successful.
The command to spend is joined to protection from the self's stinginess and then to falah, spelling out the moral work of the paid share.
Those who prefer others despite their own need and are protected from avarice are called the successful, linking gift to falah.
A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven, continuing 64:16's spending-and-success sequence with increase and cleansing.
A right for the asker and deprived person is located within the righteous person's wealth, matching the product's due rather than a voluntary leftover.
The worshippers' wealth contains a recognized due, a close counterpart to the known portion that must leave the harvest.
The recognized due is assigned to the asker and the deprived, naming those for whom the share is held.
The command to give kin, the poor, and the traveler their due generalizes the harvest command's language of a right that must be paid.
Concealed charity to the poor is called better and is said to remove evil deeds, directly pairing a paid share with cleansing.
Men and women who give charity and lend God a good loan receive multiplied return, making gift the source of increase.
Whoever purifies himself does so for his own benefit, and the destination is God; this restates tazakka as a self-returning cultivation for the lasting end.
No one would become pure without God's grace and mercy, matching the dictionary claim that true growth comes from divine blessing.
Moses asks Pharaoh whether he will purify himself, turning tazakka into the direct invitation that precedes guidance and fear.
Guidance to the Lord is meant to produce fear, joining the purification invitation to the receptive, fearing hearer of 87:10.
The rebuked assumption that the blind man might purify himself directly connects reception of the message with tazakka.
The alternative that he might take heed and benefit from the reminder connects that purification to the reminder of 87:9-10.
The successful sequence begins with one who gives and fears, uniting the paid share with the fearing hearer.
The giver seeks only the face of his Lord, the Most High, joining purified giving to رَبِّكَ ٱلْأَعْلَى.
Those who perform zakat are also certain of the afterlife, combining the share with the field toward which it is sown.
The people just described by zakat and afterlife certainty are declared the successful.
Believing men and women support one another, establish prayer, and give zakat before the promised mercy and garden reward.
Their promised gardens and enduring dwellings turn the preceding zakat into a lasting, fruitful destination and call that the great success.
One does not attain enduring goodness until giving from what one loves, specifying the costly share by which good is reached.
Full measure and weight and refusal to diminish people's goods explain the just dealing whose God-given remainder is called better in 11:86.
What people possess runs out while what is with God remains, stating the permanence within the section's definition of falah.
Worldly wealth is adornment, while enduring righteous deeds are better with the Lord in reward and hope, closely echoing خير and بقاء together.
After God increases the guided in guidance, enduring righteous deeds are better with the Lord in reward and return.
The magicians say God is better and more enduring, the exact value pair that their later purification reward in 20:76 embodies.
Worldly gifts are temporary adornment, whereas what is with God is better and more enduring.
Worldly provisions are temporary enjoyment, while what is with God is better and more enduring for trusting believers.
Everything upon the earth is passing away, giving the cultivated world's produce its widest temporal boundary.
The face of the majestic Lord remains after earthly things pass, identifying the only final permanence sought by the giver in 92:20.
God splits the grain and date-stone and brings living from dead, placing divine opening at the seed inside the section's split field.
Water produces vegetation, layered grain, and ripening fruit, and the reader is told to look at fruiting and maturity; this is the field's growth made visible.
Joseph commands seven years of sowing and leaving the harvested grain in its ears except a little eaten, a concrete picture of yield and preserved remainder.
The parable's two vineyards, palms, and intervening crop form a fully cultivated estate rather than wild pasture.
Both gardens give their fruit without withholding anything, presenting complete yield before the owner's failure.
The owner enters his garden and claims it will never perish, mistaking a fruitful field for an inherently lasting possession.
The believing companion says entry into the garden should acknowledge God's will and power, naming the stance proper to received growth.
He warns that his Lord can give something better and send a calamity that leaves the garden barren and slippery.
The garden's water may sink beyond recovery, exposing the hidden provision on which its growth depends.
The fruit is encompassed and its owner wrings his hands over ruined trellises, a cultivated yield reduced to loss.
God sends water and grows beautiful gardens whose trees humans could not grow, directly assigning the finished cultivation to Him.
Water is driven to barren land and brings out crops eaten by livestock and people, changing dead ground into provision.
Dead earth is revived and grain is brought from it for people to eat, a compact field sequence of opening, growth, and benefit.
Gardens of palms and grapes and flowing springs turn the revived soil into cultivated abundance.
People eat the gardens' fruit though their hands did not create it, pressing the distinction between farmer and divine Grower.
The sky characterized by returning rain supplies the water paired with the split earth in the next ayah.
The earth characterized by splitting, ٱلْأَرْضِ ذَاتِ ٱلصَّدْعِ, is a compressed parallel to water poured and ground opened for growth.
Burying or corrupting the soul ends in failure, the direct negative counterpart to successful purification and, in the section's field reading, to growth smothered underground.
Charity spoiled by display and injury is like thin soil washed from rock by rain, a gift whose apparent field retains no yield.
A fruit garden is burned by a fiery whirlwind when its owner is most vulnerable, showing cultivated abundance without lasting security.
The corrupt person destroys cultivated land and progeny, reversing the Lord-like work of maintaining and repairing a farm.
Worldly spending by wrongdoers is like a freezing wind that destroys a crop, an anti-harvest opposite to charity that multiplies.
Worldly life is a rain-grown field whose owners think it mastered, then God's command leaves it as mown as if it had never flourished.
A corrupt word is an uprooted bad tree with no stability, the plant-image opposite to growth that remains in good.
Worldly life is rain-grown vegetation that becomes dry fragments scattered by wind, directly aligning the nearer life with transient growth.
God waters varied crops, then they yellow and become debris; the complete cycle distinguishes visible growth from what lasts.
The nearer life's growth delights the cultivators, then withers, yellows, and becomes debris before the ayah turns to the afterlife.
When the people of Saba turn away, their two fruitful gardens are replaced by bitter produce, tamarisk, and sparse lote trees.
The ban on multiplied usury ends with the call to fear God so that one may attain falah, opposing grasped increase to purified success.
People who claim purity for themselves are corrected: God purifies whom He wills, a boundary on treating tazakka as self-produced growth.
The command not to declare oneself pure makes God's knowledge of the truly fearing person the measure of purification.
The one who withholds and deems himself self-sufficient begins the exact reverse of the giver's purifying course.
Denying the best outcome supplies the inward counterpart to withholding the share.
The withholder is eased toward hardship, reversing both the giver's ease and the productive field's good end.
Those called to spend who remain stingy only harm themselves, while God is rich; withheld produce therefore cannot secure its holder.
The growers' stunned lament is the human response to the crop being turned into chaff and keeps 56:65 inside a farmer's experience.
Their harvest oath allows no exception; the wording marks an absolute claim over a crop whose divine and human claims they ignore.
Affirming the best outcome explains why the giver in 92:5 can treat what leaves his hand as seed for a better end.
The giver who fears and affirms the best is promised ease, linking the share's path to the promise of ease in surah 87.
The most God-fearing person is kept away from the fire before his wealth-giving purification is identified in 92:18.
The giver is not repaying another person's favor, clarifying that the purifying gift is not an ordinary exchange for worldly return.
The purified giver is promised satisfaction, completing the good end of the wealth that was released.
God promises to replace whatever is spent, a non-agricultural statement of the share returning as provision rather than depletion.
Prayer, zakat, and a good loan are followed by the promise that whatever good is sent ahead will be found with God better and greater in reward.
Flood foam vanishes while what benefits people remains on earth, a parallel sorting of waste from the beneficial remainder.
Rain is carried to dead land and brings out every fruit, supplying the divine watering behind the good and bad soils compared in 7:58.
Hard years consume the stored harvest except a little kept back, making the preserved remainder the field's means of survival.
A year of rain and pressing produce restores yield after famine, completing the managed crop cycle.
A good word is a good tree with firm root and high branch, an organic image of goodness made stable.
That tree gives fruit every season by its Lord's permission, making persistence in good a recurring yield.
God-sent water supplies drink and grows the vegetation in which livestock pasture, locating field and pasture under one provision.
The same water grows crops, olives, palms, grapes, and every fruit, a broad inventory of blessed cultivated growth.
Possession of abundant fruit leads the garden owner to boast in wealth and followers, exposing the worldly preference attached to the yield.
He doubts the Hour and assumes an even better return if restored to his Lord, carrying false confidence in the garden into the afterlife.
After the garden's collapse, true protection belongs to God, who is better in reward and outcome; this identifies the lasting good the owner missed.
God makes the earth serviceable, sends water, and brings out diverse pairs of plants, echoing the One who tends and brings forth the field.
People are told to eat and pasture their livestock from that growth, specifying the crop's beneficiaries.
Barren earth stirs, swells, and grows every beautiful pair when rain falls, turning hidden life into visible increase.
Water descends in measured amount and is lodged in the earth, while God can remove it; the field's source is both apportioned and precarious.
That measured water produces palm and grape gardens with abundant fruit from which people eat.
The Sinai tree supplies oil and food, adding a useful harvested product to the gardens of 23:19.
The question directs attention to how many noble plant-pairs God has grown from the earth, another command to read the ground's yield.
Rain makes every noble kind grow on earth, assigning variety and increase to divine action.
Saba's two gardens are a sign and provision from a good land under a forgiving Lord, a field explicitly held within gratitude.
The replacement of the gardens is named recompense for ingratitude, defining the moral boundary exposed by their lost yield.
Humbled earth stirs and swells when water falls, showing growth as revival by the One who gives life.
Blessed rain grows gardens and harvest grain, bringing divine provision to the point of reaping.
Tall palms with layered clusters specify the mature produce of the rain-grown scene.
The harvest is provision for servants and revival for dead land, naming both beneficiary and source of renewed growth.
Abundant poured water begins a sequence that closely parallels 80:25-31.
God brings out grain and vegetation through that water, making the rain productive.
Dense gardens complete the water, grain, and growth sequence as cultivated abundance.
The people offer a kharj in exchange for protective work; this payment sense illuminates the section's named kharj/kharaj branch without itself being a crop due.
People are made successors over wealth and commanded to spend from it, fitting the field's Lord as true owner and the cultivator as steward.
A good loan to God is multiplied many times, expressing the paid share as increase held beyond the immediate possession.
The good loan that God multiplies gives the share a promised return and generous reward.
Whatever good is spent benefits the giver and will be repaid in full, explaining how released wealth is not finally lost.
The Messenger and believers strive with wealth and lives, receive good things, and are called the successful; it is a distinct wealth-to-falah route.
Prayer, zakat, and a good loan are followed by cleansing of evils and entry into rivered gardens, joining the share, purification, and lasting yield.
The believing speaker calls worldly life brief enjoyment and the afterlife the settled home, a plain gloss on transient versus abiding gain.
Worldly life is diversion while the afterlife is the true life, clarifying which field's growth counts as lasting life.
People love the immediate life, naming the preference that makes worldly cultivation the chosen field.
They leave the afterlife, completing the same choice between the two fields stated agriculturally in 42:20.
Loving the immediate life and leaving a weighty day behind repeats the preference that makes temporary yield seem sufficient.
Preferring worldly life is singled out as the decisive choice on the destructive side of the final outcome.
Fearing the station of one's Lord and restraining desire gives the opposite stance, recalling the one who fears and accepts purification.
The garden is the refuge for that fearing restraint, giving the successful choice a cultivated destination.
The answer to what should be spent is العفو, commonly understood as what can be spared; this may illuminate a measured share that leaves a sound remainder, though it is not a harvest rule.
One pilgrim asks only for worldly benefit and consequently has no share in the afterlife, closely matching the worldly tilth with no afterlife portion in 42:20.
The contrasting prayer asks for good in both the world and the afterlife, refusing to make the nearer field the sole crop.
Those who ask for both goods receive a share of what they have earned, joining labor, portion, and lasting outcome.
Cultivated land is listed among the alluring provisions of worldly life, making the field itself one object of the preference named in 87:16.
What is better than those worldly attractions is then identified as abiding gardens with the Lord, turning cultivation toward its lasting end.
The idolaters assign invented portions of crops to God and partners, a precise corruption of the harvest's true due.
God is said to accept repentance and take charities, identifying the Lord as the ultimate receiver of the share released from wealth.
Those who desire worldly life and its adornment are paid their works in full here, a crop intentionally confined to the nearer field.
For those worldly workers nothing remains in the afterlife but fire and their works become void, stating the failed permanence of that harvest.
God spreads the earth and causes every well-balanced thing to grow in it, joining cultivation to fitting measure.
God's treasuries release everything only in a known measure, closely matching the section's measured outgoing share and divine provision.
Full measure and just weight are commanded and called better in outcome, clarifying how a due is paid without corrupting the remainder.
The faithful neither squander nor withhold when spending but keep a measured middle, a boundary around both the paid share and what remains.
God-given wealth is to seek the afterlife while retaining one's worldly share and avoiding corruption, a direct statement of how one provision is sown toward the lasting field.
God is said to have caused human beings to grow from the earth as a plant, extending the section's cultivated growth to the person who purifies himself.
Woe is declared for those who defraud in measure, the commercial opposite of giving the produce's rightful portion.
The defrauders demand full measure when receiving from others, exposing grasping at the incoming share.
When measuring or weighing for others they diminish it, directly reversing payment of the known due.
The condemned person gathers wealth and repeatedly counts it, holding the whole yield rather than releasing its claim.
He imagines that his wealth makes him permanent, the false worldly version of the section's abiding good.
Rain brings fruits from the earth as provision, a compact divine field scene in which the product is received rather than self-created.
Those who spend without reminders or injury retain their reward, specifying conduct by which a gift's fruit is not spoiled.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, marking a boundary between cleansing gift and morally damaged gift.
Mary's Lord accepts her graciously and makes her grow with good growth, an explicit human counterpart to divinely blessed cultivation.
Those who withhold God's bounty mistake stinginess for good, but what they hoard becomes a burden, reversing the good remainder produced by giving.
Worldly enjoyment is called little and the afterlife better for the God-fearing, tying the better field to the same fearing stance as 87:10.
Worldly life is play and diversion while the afterlife home is better for those who fear, another specific statement of the two valuations behind the field choice.
Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it are warned, a concrete reversal of wealth released in purification.
The addressees are asked whether they are content with worldly life instead of the afterlife and are told its enjoyment is slight.
The afterlife home is called better for those who fear, repeating the link between fear and the better lasting destination.
People rejoice in worldly life even though it is only a passing enjoyment beside the afterlife, distinguishing temporary provision from final gain.
God sends down water and brings out fruits as provision, assigning the field's useful yield to its Lord.
God places livelihoods on earth for people and for creatures they do not provide for, widening the beneficiaries of the measured growth in 15:19.
Fertilizing winds and water from heaven are supplied while humans do not control its stores, locating crop growth in divine husbandry.
Those receptive to their Lord's revelation are promised good here and a better home in the afterlife, repeating the better destination of good action.
Whoever wants the immediate life receives only what God chooses before reaching a destructive end, defining one deliberately short-term cultivation.
Whoever seeks the afterlife with fitting effort and faith has that effort appreciated, the active counterpart to sowing for the afterlife.
The prohibition on squandering immediately after giving each claimant his due prevents payment of the share from becoming waste.
David and Solomon judge a crop damaged at night by sheep, a concrete boundary of responsibility around cultivated yield.
Rain makes the earth green under God's subtle care, a concise image of hidden provision becoming visible growth.
God sends pure water from heaven, placing purity itself at the source of the revival described in the next ayah.
That water revives dead land and gives drink to animals and people, joining purification, growth, and provision.
The command to give full measure and not be among those who diminish restates the justice required when a known portion leaves one's goods.
Straight weighing specifies the honest measurement by which the due is separated.
People's goods must not be diminished and the earth must not be corrupted, extending just measurement into the care of the ground itself.
Rain brings forth fruits of varied colors, another direct formulation of the Lord producing the field's yield.
Water descends in a measured amount and revives dead land, linking measure, provision, and renewed growth.
Provision descends from heaven and revives the earth after death, making the productive field one of the signs to be understood.
People are commanded to spend from provision before death makes them wish for time to give charity, placing a firm limit on when the share can bear fruit.
The righteous give desired food to the poor, orphan, and captive, turning provision itself into the released share.
They feed only for God's face and seek neither repayment nor thanks, matching the purified giver's motive in 92:20.
